method: One procedure, fitted on the public training pages only. (1) A glyph chain over the whole line, with the word space and the line end as ordinary symbols; each glyph is drawn given the four symbols before it, or, 6 times in 10, given only the two before it. It starts afresh at each line, from one start mark for a line that opens a paragraph and another for any other line. (2) The table drifts: the writer plans a book of 780 lines (15% of the manuscript's lines, the size of a sample of pages) and at each point uses counts from a window of 20 consecutive public pages that slides from the first page to the last as the book goes on (40 steps; the whole-text table is mixed in at weight 0.1). Paragraph-opening lines follow the same schedule at their own pace (their share of lines on the public pages, 14%). Lines written after the planned end use the last window. (3) Two kinds of reuse at the start of a word. With probability 0.25 the writer takes one of the last 15 words written (on a paragraph-opening line, only words already on that line) and changes one glyph of it to another that the chain allows between its neighbours. With probability 0.25 (ordinary lines only) it writes again, whole, a familiar word: one that stands at least twice among the last 300 words written. In both cases it prefers a word whose first glyph the chain allows after what was just written. No rule names a glyph, a word, a position in the line other than its start, a section or a Currier language. Lines holding a four-word run of the manuscript are redrawn. 'lines' are ordinary lines, 'first_lines' paragraph-opening lines. What matters for this fact is the second kind of reuse. On the practice split (manuscript 0.311, line at 0.25): the chain with one table and no copying gives 0.20 to 0.21; with a drifting table and copies of which 19 in 20 are altered, 0.21 to 0.24 (fails); with whole copies of any recent word it passes (0.26 to 0.30) but loses the singleton share of F-014 (0.58 to 0.65); writing again only familiar words gives 0.285 here, and 0.324, 0.316 for seeds 2 and 3, 0.288 and 0.295 when fitted on every other public page only, with the singleton share at 0.69 to 0.71 in the same five texts. So the pincer this fact forms with F-014 is met by one plain habit: repeat whole the words you have already used more than once, vary the others. The same five texts meet, locally, every other established fact. Weakness: the reuse rate, the memory of 300 words and the threshold of two were set on the public practice split with this fact and F-014 in view; an earlier setting of this very rule (copies taken from the last 15 words only) met both and then overshot the repetition from the line above, so the rule was changed once more before this text was made.
